To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have profiled the binding affinity and epitopes of a panel of mouse anti‐CD‐40 monoclonal antibody, and we have correlated the affinity and epitopes with their ability to activate CD40‐expressing cells.
we have profiled mouse anti‐CD4 antibodies regarding their CD40L binding affinity and epitopicity, and we have shown that there is no correlation between binding affinity and cellular activation.

the CD40‐binding affinities and epitope‐binding specificities of a panel of mouse anti‐CD4 monoclonal antibodies are highly heterogeneous and that this is related to their capacity to activate B‐cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the generation and characterization of antibodies against human CD40.

the production of humanized anti‐CD40 MoAbs with the potential to be developed into therapeutic antibodies for the treatment of autoimmune diseases, such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA).
the generation of antibodies against the CD40 receptor.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no correlation between affinity for CD40 and activation potential of CD40‐specific antibodies.
the epitope‐specific binding to the CD40 molecule does not seem to be a major determinant for the ability of a given anti‐CD40 antibody to activate B‐cells.

there is no correlation between the ability of a CD40‐binding antibody to activate a B cell and its affinity for CD40, but rather that the ability to block the binding of CD40L is a more important determinant of the activation potential.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the CD40 binding epitope is a rather large area on the CD40 molecule.

the affinity of a CD40‐binding antibody does not predict its ability to activate B cells, but that the ability to block the CD40L‐CD40 interaction correlates well with the activation potential of the antibody.
the epitope‐specificities of anti‐CD40 monoclonal antibody are important in the regulation of the CD40–CD4L interaction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is not sufficient to simply determine the binding epitope and binding affinity to CD40 for the development of new therapeutic antibodies.
affinity and epitope specificity are not necessarily the main factors determining the ability of a given CD40 antibody to induce or block B cell proliferation.
the CD40‐binding epitope is a very important factor for antibody‐mediated CD40 activation and blocking.
